title: Measuring Verifier Impact in an LLM Generate→Verify→Repair Loop for Intent→Configuration NetOps Tasks
abstract: We measure how inserting a deterministic network verifier into a generate→verify→repair (G→V→R) loop changes verifier-detected safety violations of LLM-produced device-configuration proposals. In a preregistered paired design (N = 500 intent→configuration tasks stratified across VLAN-change, ACL-change, and static-route-change clusters) we compared: (1) baseline — a single LLM proposal produced once per task (requested model: gpt-5-mini), and (2) guarded — the identical shared proposal validated by a deterministic netops validator with up to one automated repair iteration invoked only if the validator reported a preregistered high/medium-severity violation. Primary outcome: verifier pass (no preregistered high/medium-severity violations). Results (complete pairs = 500): baseline passed 499/500 (0.998), guarded passed 500/500 (1.000); contingency: n11 = 499, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Absolute paired success-rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.002. The archived analysis used the exact McNemar two-sided convention implemented as an exact binomial on discordant pairs (n = n10 + n01), yielding two-sided p = 1.00 for the observed single discordant pair. Paired-bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.0, 0.006] (B = 10,000, seed = 1729). Interpretation: on this verifier-scoped synthetic corpus and model+validator pairing the LLM produced near-ceiling proposals; the marginal numeric verifier+repair effect on the pass-rate metric is therefore small, though one archived discordant episode shows the loop corrected a concrete baseline failure. All preregistration, prompts, model outputs, validator traces, provider-call traces, execution logs, and analysis artifacts are archived and referenced in the Disclosure Statement.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are being applied to NetOps tasks such as translating operator intent into device configuration, planning multi-step changes, and generating repair proposals. System reports and recent surveys emphasize that operational safety commonly depends on surrounding engineering—deterministic validators, sandbox replay, canarying, rollback—rather than on the model alone [Beckett et al., 2017; Wei et al., 2025; Bilal et al., 2026]. A widely proposed mitigation is generate→verify→repair (G→V→R): the model generates a candidate, a deterministic verifier checks formalized properties, and repairs are applied when violations appear. Despite conceptual agreement, controlled measurements that isolate the verifier’s marginal contribution while holding the model’s proposal fixed are scarce.

We preregistered and executed a confirmatory paired experiment to quantify that marginal contribution under disciplined constraints. Our primary question (preregistered) is: How much does integrating a deterministic verifier plus a single automated repair iteration reduce verifier-detected safety violations in LLM-generated device-configuration proposals compared to the same LLM alone, when the initial proposal is fixed (shared-initial_candidate semantics)? The preregistration, execution manifests, raw outputs, and analysis artifacts were archived and form the empirical evidence for every numeric claim below.
sections.related_work: Formal and deterministic network-configuration verifiers and route-model checkers (header-space analyses, Batfish-style verifiers) can detect reachability, isolation, and update-safety violations and are widely used in NetOps verification research [Beckett et al., 2017]. Recent NetOps/AIOps systems propose LLM-based intent translators and consistently argue for validators and guardrails to attain operational reliability (e.g., INTA, Confucius, and several 2025–2026 system reports) [Wei et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025; Bilal et al., 2026]. Generate–verify–repair patterns have been proposed across structured-generation domains to reduce incorrect outputs and produce machine-checkable artifacts [Qu et al., 2026; INTA]. Failure-mode studies document hallucinations, overconfidence, and tool-integration failures that motivate verifier-in-the-loop pipelines [Owen, 2026; DeepSeek-AI, 2025]. However, the supplied literature rarely contains preregistered, artifact-backed ablations that quantify a verifier’s effect size conditional on identical model proposals; this study contributes one such controlled measurement and situates it relative to prior system proposals.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and design: The experiment was preregistered (study_id cand_7f4b9a2d_hosted_gvr_v1_2026) and froze the research question, inclusion/exclusion rules, task-generation seeds, estimands, analysis executor, multiplicity plan, retry policy, and stopping rule before execution. Primary confirmatory hypothesis: a deterministic verifier plus a single automated repair iteration will produce a lower verifier-detected safety-violation rate than the same LLM producing a single proposal without verifier feedback (paired per task). The primary estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline where success == verifier reports zero preregistered high/medium-severity violations.

Task corpus and strata: We generated a deterministic synthetic corpus of 500 intent→configuration tasks using deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 with preregistered seeds. Tasks were stratified into VLAN-change (167), ACL-change (167), and static-route-change (166) clusters. To preserve construct validity relative to the verifier, task generator constraints limited allowed_fields to {admin, mtu, vlan}. Per-preregistration, tasks referencing unmodeled features would be routed to an "unmodeled-feature" cohort and excluded from the primary analysis; no confirmatory exclusions occurred.

Generation semantics and experimental control: Crucially, we used generation_semantics = "shared_initial_candidate" with independent_condition_generation = false. For each task the pipeline produced one shared LLM proposal (the shared candidate). The baseline condition observes that proposal as the model-only output; the guarded condition validates the identical shared proposal and invokes the repair-stage call only when the deterministic validator reports a preregistered high/medium-severity violation on that shared candidate. This semantic isolates the marginal effect of verification and a single repair iteration given identical proposals and avoids conflating verifier effects with verifier-guided regeneration strategies (which answer a different operational question).

Models, adapter, and validator: Requested LLM = gpt-5-mini (provider recorded as openai_responses) called through the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter; model configuration (max_output_tokens = 2000, single-attempt generation) is archived. The deterministic verifier was deterministic_netops_validator_v5; its validator-spec and the mapping from violation codes to severities are archived in the evidence bundle. The guarded arm permitted at most one automated repair iteration per preregistration.

Primary statistical test and exact implementation: The preregistered confirmatory test was an exact McNemar two-sided test on paired binary outcomes. Our archived analysis executor implements the standard exact McNemar by treating the number of discordant pairs n = n10 + n01 and performing an exact binomial test on the observed count n10 under X ∼ Binomial(n, 0.5). For a two-sided p-value the executor computes p_two-sided = 2 × min{P(X ≤ n10), P(X ≥ n10)} and truncates at 1.0. The executor also reports paired-bootstrap percentile confidence intervals (B = 10,000 resamples, seed = 1729, resampling unit = task/pair while preserving pairing). The precise implementation details and code parameters are archived in analysis/analysis_log.jsonl.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and primary outcomes: The run completed with complete_pair_count = 500 and model_calls_used = 501 (shared_initial_generation = 500 and repair-stage calls = 1). Aggregated per-condition counts (analysis/condition_summary.csv) are: baseline successes = 499, baseline failures = 1 (baseline_success_rate = 0.998); guarded successes = 500, guarded failures = 0 (guarded_success_rate = 1.000). The paired contingency table (guarded × baseline) is: n11 = 499, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Absolute paired success-rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.002.

Exact McNemar and bootstrap CI: Using the archived exact-binomial convention on discordant pairs (n = 1) the two-sided p-value is computed as p = 2 × min{0.5, 0.5} = 1.00; this arises because with a single discordant pair the two tails each have probability 0.5 under the null X ∼ Binomial(1, 0.5) and the two-sided rule doubles the smaller tail, producing 1.00 after truncation. The paired-bootstrap percentile 95% CI for the absolute difference is [0.0, 0.006] (B = 10,000, seed = 1729). Both the p-value and CI are archived in analysis/results.json and accompanied CSV artifacts.

Repair activity and discordant-pair provenance: Observed repair-stage provider calls = 1 across the run; that single repair produced the sole discordant outcome (n10 = 1). The per-task validator diagnostics, normalized configurations, repair prompts/responses (when invoked), and provider-call traces are archived in execution/raw_results.jsonl and related scoring artifacts. The unique discordant episode can be located deterministically by filtering execution/raw_results.jsonl for pair entries where the baseline scoring indicates a preregistered high/medium-severity violation (baseline pass == 0) while the guarded scoring indicates pass == 1; because exactly one such discordant pair exists this filter returns the single episode and its repair-stage trace. The validator violation-code→severity mapping that classifies that baseline outcome is archived in the validator-spec artifact and the execution manifest. Representative per-task examples and provider-call traces for several tasks are included among the execution artifact examples.

Secondary analyses and power mismatch: The preregistered per-violation-class secondary analyses were uninformative because observed violation counts were nearly zero—there were no sufficient counts to support class-level inference. The preregistration's power planning assumed a baseline error prevalence near p_b ≈ 0.30 (needed N ≈ 384 for 80% power to detect a 10 percentage-point absolute reduction). The observed baseline success rate (499/500) produced a ceiling effect that undermined sensitivity to detect small absolute improvements on the pass-rate metric. Analysis artifacts include a missingness_summary.csv and a contamination_summary.csv; both indicate no exclusions, no missing pairs, and no contamination events in this run.
sections.discussion:
Operational interpretation: This experiment quantifies the marginal verifier+single-repair effect under a constrained operational regime: a single requested LLM (gpt-5-mini), shared_initial_candidate semantics, a deterministic validator modeling a limited property set (allowed_fields = {admin, mtu, vlan}), and a single automated repair iteration. Under these constraints the LLM produced near-ceiling correct proposals and the measured absolute improvement on the pass-rate metric was therefore small (0.002). Importantly, the result should not be read to imply verifiers are unnecessary. The verifier corrected at least one concrete baseline failure (the single discordant episode), demonstrating corrective potential; in workloads with higher baseline error prevalence, broader property coverage, heterogeneous vendor CLIs, or different generation semantics, verifier+repair gains may be much larger.

Design-choice consequences and semantics: The shared_initial_candidate semantics intentionally isolates verifier+repair effect conditional on identical proposals; it answers the specific operational question: what is the additional safety provided by a verifier+single-repair when the model’s proposal is fixed? It does not measure the effect of verifier-guided regeneration, multi-iteration repair budgets, or independent-condition generation. Each semantics maps to a different operational tradeoff (minimal-change deployments vs. maximizing final-pass probability) and practitioners should match experiments to deployment semantics.

Threats to validity: Internal validity is supported by the preregistered paired design, deterministic generation seeds, automatic exclusion rules, and fully archived execution logs. Construct validity is limited by the verifier’s modeled property set and by the synthetic task generator constraints (allowed_fields = {admin, mtu, vlan}). External validity is limited by the single requested model and single validator; results do not imply multi-model or cross-vendor generality. Conclusion validity is constrained by the ceiling effect: with baseline failures near zero the confirmatory McNemar test has low sensitivity to detect small absolute gains; the exact two-sided p = 1.00 reflects that low sensitivity given the observed discordant counts and the archived two-sided binomial convention.

Operational recommendations: (1) Measure baseline proposal error prevalence on representative production data before allocating expensive automated-repair budgets: when baseline error is extremely low, marginal pass-rate improvements from verifier+repair may be small on pass-rate metrics. (2) Align verifier property coverage with operator safety priorities; the validator-spec and severity mapping in the evidence bundle allow operators to inspect coverage relative to local requirements. (3) Select generation semantics (shared-initial vs verifier-guided regeneration) that reflect deployment priorities: shared-initial minimizes model-regeneration cost and measures conditional verifier impact; verifier-guided regeneration optimizes final pass probability at the expense of additional model calls and latency. The evidence bundle includes exemplar repair traces and provider-call accounting to support cost–benefit evaluations.
sections.conclusion: We report a preregistered, artifact-backed paired experiment (N = 500) that isolated the verifier+single-repair effect under shared_initial_candidate semantics. The LLM produced near-ceiling correct proposals (baseline 499/500; guarded 500/500), yielding an absolute improvement of 0.002 (95% CI [0.0, 0.006]; archived exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00 under the executor convention). The archive shows one concrete correction by the guarded loop (one repair-stage call). The measurement documents a ceiling-effect regime: when baseline proposal error prevalence is very low and verifier coverage is constrained, the measured marginal pass-rate benefit of a verifier on this metric may be negligible even while the verifier can still correct rare concrete failures. Operators should measure baseline error prevalence, align verifier coverage to operational safety needs, and choose regeneration/repair semantics that match deployment priorities. Full preregistration, raw outputs, validator traces, repair traces, execution logs, and analysis artifacts are archived and referenced in the Disclosure Statement for deterministic re-inspection and follow-up analyses.

limitations: Synthetic, deterministic task corpus limited to features modeled by the deterministic validator; task payloads in the archive show allowed_fields = {admin, mtu, vlan}. Results do not necessarily generalize to unconstrained production intents, cross-vendor CLI heterogeneity, or protocol semantics outside the verifier scope.
Single model family tested (gpt-5-mini requested) and a single validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) — no claim of multi-model generality is made.
Maximum one automated repair iteration was permitted by the preregistration; different repair budgets or iterative regeneration strategies could change measured verifier impact.

Very high baseline pass rate (499/500) created a ceiling effect that limits power to detect small absolute improvements on the pass-rate metric; the archived exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00 reflects the two-sided exact-binomial convention for n = 1 discordant pair and must be interpreted in that context.

The single discordant episode (the sole task where baseline failed and guarded succeeded) and its validator diagnostics and repair-stage trace are archived in execution/raw_results.jsonl in the evidence bundle. To inspect it deterministically: filter execution/raw_results.jsonl for pair entries where the baseline scoring outcome indicates a preregistered high/medium-severity violation (baseline pass == 0) while the guarded scoring outcome indicates pass == 1; because only one such discordant pair exists in the confirmatory set, this lookup returns the single episode and its provider-call traces. The validator violation-code→severity mapping is archived in the execution manifest and validator-spec artifacts in the bundle.
